whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the JavaScript Developer I exam for?

personas.label: Web developers moving into Salesforce
personas.description: Your JavaScript is already good. What you need is the component model, the Apex boundary and the security rules.

personas.label: Salesforce developers who came from Apex
personas.description: This is the exam that exposes self-taught JavaScript. The language half is where the marks go, not the LWC half.

personas.label: Anyone who writes Lightning Web Components
personas.description: Whether or not you want the credential, the syllabus is a reasonable list of what you should know to write components that behave.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the JavaScript Developer I Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: A JavaScript exam that happens to run on Salesforce. Most of it is language fundamentals: scope, closures, prototypes, promises, the event loop, and reading code to say what it prints. The Salesforce content is real but smaller. Platform developers who learned JavaScript as they went tend to find this harder than they expect.
bullets: 60 questions in 105 minutes. Code-reading questions eat time, so do not spend five minutes on one snippet.
65% to pass, leaving roughly 19 you can get wrong.
Execution order is the recurring theme. Promises are microtasks, setTimeout is a macrotask, and a snippet mixing them is a near certainty.
The LWC half is lifecycle and data. connectedCallback against renderedCallback, wire against imperative Apex, and how events cross the shadow boundary.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Open a console and predict the output before you run it. Closures in loops, a promise chain with a setTimeout in the middle, this inside a regular function against an arrow function. If you get those right consistently, the exam will not surprise you. If not, that is where to spend your week.

examFormat.heading: JavaScript Developer I Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: Proctored online or at a test centre. The shape of it:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Close to half the questions involve code. Usually it is a snippet with a question about what it logs, in what order, or why it throws. The rest is choosing the right decorator, lifecycle hook or async pattern for a stated requirement.
bestWayToPass: Write the code, do not read about it. Every topic on this syllabus can be tested in a browser console in under a minute. Guess the output first, then run it.

Learn the event loop properly. Call stack, microtask queue, macrotask queue. Once you can place a promise callback and a setTimeout callback on the right queue, the ordering questions become mechanical.
Know what this binds to in each case. Method call, standalone function, arrow function, callback passed to another function. Four cases, asked repeatedly.
Build one component that calls Apex both ways. Once with wire, once imperatively from a button. The difference between them stops being abstract.

certificationCard.description: Core JavaScript and the Lightning Web Components model: ES6 syntax, scope and closures, prototypes, promises and async/await, the event loop, the web component standards LWC is built on, calling Apex, and Lightning Web Security.

keyConcepts.h2: JavaScript Developer I: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Scope, Closures and this
blocks.body: A closure is a function that keeps access to the variables of the scope it was created in, even after that scope has returned. It is the mechanism behind private state, factory functions and most callback bugs. The classic exam case is a loop that creates functions: with var, every function shares one binding and they all see the final value, while let creates a fresh binding each iteration and they see what you expected. Separately, this is decided by how a function is called rather than where it is written. Called as a method, this is the object. Called standalone, it is undefined in strict mode. In an arrow function, there is no own this at all, so it comes from the enclosing scope, which is exactly why arrow functions are used for callbacks that need the surrounding context. Expect a snippet where a method is passed as a callback and loses its binding.

blocks.heading: Prototypes and Classes
blocks.body: JavaScript inheritance works through a chain of objects. Every object has a prototype, and a property lookup walks up that chain until it finds the property or runs out. Class syntax is a cleaner way of writing the same thing: a class body defines methods on the prototype, extends sets up the chain, and super calls the parent. Two details are examinable. Methods defined in the class body live on the prototype and are shared across instances, whereas properties assigned in the constructor belong to each instance. And instanceof asks whether a prototype appears anywhere in an object's chain, which is why it answers true for an inherited type as well as the exact one.

blocks.heading: Promises, async/await and Error Handling
blocks.body: A promise is an object representing a result that has not arrived. It settles once, either resolved or rejected, and then handlers registered with then, catch and finally run. Chaining matters because each then returns a new promise, so returning a value passes it along and returning a promise waits for it. async and await are syntax over the same thing: an async function always returns a promise, and await pauses inside it until the awaited promise settles. For error handling, a rejection travels down a chain until something catches it, and an uncaught rejection is a silent failure you should treat as a bug. The combinators get asked by behaviour: Promise.all rejects as soon as any input rejects, Promise.allSettled always resolves and reports each outcome, and Promise.race settles with whichever finishes first.

blocks.heading: The Event Loop
blocks.body: JavaScript runs one thing at a time. Synchronous code runs to completion on the call stack. When the stack empties, the runtime drains the microtask queue, which is where promise callbacks go; and only then takes one task from the macrotask queue, which is where setTimeout and setInterval callbacks go. That ordering is the whole answer to most execution-order questions: all synchronous logging first, then promise callbacks, then timer callbacks, even a setTimeout with a delay of zero. It is also why a long synchronous loop freezes the page, since nothing else can run until the stack clears. Knowing this one model well is worth more marks than any other single topic on the exam.

blocks.heading: Lightning Web Components: Lifecycle, Apex and Security
blocks.body: LWC is built on web component standards, so a component is a custom element with its own shadow tree. The lifecycle hooks have specific moments: constructor runs before the component is in the DOM and must not touch it, connectedCallback runs when it is inserted and is where you start work that does not need rendered markup, renderedCallback runs after every render and so must guard against repeating itself, and disconnectedCallback is where you clean up subscriptions and listeners. For data, the wire service is declarative and reactive: it fetches when its parameters change and is right for reading. Imperative calls are made from JavaScript when you need control over timing, such as on a button click, or when the call changes data. Events travel up: by default an event raised inside a shadow tree does not cross the boundary unless it is created with composed true, which is why custom events are usually handled by the immediate parent. Lightning Web Security replaced LockerService and restricts what component code can reach, including direct DOM access outside the component's own tree.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce JavaScript Developer I Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Treat the language half as the exam and the platform half as a supplement. Nearly everything here is testable in a console in under a minute.

blocks.heading: Predict, Then Run
blocks.body: Write snippets, guess the output, then execute. This single habit covers closures, hoisting, this binding and execution order.

blocks.heading: The Three Queues
blocks.body: Call stack, then microtasks, then one macrotask. Promise callbacks beat setTimeout every time, including setTimeout zero.

blocks.heading: Four Cases for this
blocks.body: Method call, standalone call, arrow function, and a method passed as a callback. Know what this is in each.

blocks.heading: Promise Combinators by Behaviour
blocks.body: all rejects fast, allSettled never rejects, race settles first. Questions describe the behaviour rather than naming the method.

blocks.heading: Lifecycle Hooks by Timing
blocks.body: connectedCallback for setup without the DOM, renderedCallback after every render so guard it, disconnectedCallback for cleanup.

sampleQuestions.question: Which JavaScript feature is used to handle asynchronous operations without blocking the main thread?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Promises and async/await are the modern JavaScript approach for handling asynchronous operations.
whyWrong: Synchronous loops block the main thread, the opposite of what's needed for async handling.
var is a variable declaration keyword, unrelated to asynchronous operations.
Callbacks alone are an older async pattern; Promises/async-await are the modern standard tested on this exam.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the primary use of Lightning Web Components (LWC) in the Salesforce ecosystem?
options: Building reactive UI components that run on the Lightning Platform
sampleQuestions.explanation: LWC is the standard for building performant, reusable UI components on the Salesforce Lightning Platform.
whyWrong: Email templates are unrelated to LWC's purpose as a UI component framework.
Data modeling is a separate concern from building UI components.
LWC runs on the client (browser) side, not as backend Apex logic.

sampleQuestions.question: Which keyword creates a block-scoped variable in JavaScript?
sampleQuestions.explanation: let (and const) create block-scoped variables; var is function-scoped.
whyWrong: function declares a function, not a variable.
var is function-scoped, not block-scoped; this is precisely why let/const were introduced.
'global' is not a JavaScript variable declaration keyword.

sampleQuestions.question: What does the shadow DOM provide in web components?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Shadow DOM provides style and markup encapsulation so component internals don't leak out.
whyWrong: Shadow DOM doesn't manage database access.
Shadow DOM has nothing to do with API keys or security credentials.
Shadow DOM is a client-side browser feature, unrelated to server-side rendering.

sampleQuestions.question: Which LWC decorator makes a property available to the component's template?
sampleQuestions.explanation: @api exposes a public property that can be set by a parent component.
whyWrong: @invocable is not an LWC decorator, it's unrelated to component properties.
@track is used for reactive private property tracking, not for exposing properties to the template/parent.
@wire is used for provisioning data from Salesforce, not for exposing properties externally.

sampleQuestions.question: Which LWC wire adapter is used to get a record by Id?
sampleQuestions.explanation: getRecord wire adapter fetches a record by Id with specified fields.
whyWrong: getListUi retrieves a list of records, not a single record by Id.
getObjectInfo retrieves object metadata, not record field data.
createRecord creates a new record, it doesn't retrieve an existing one.

sampleQuestions.question: What does the spread operator (...) do in JavaScript?
sampleQuestions.explanation: The spread operator expands arrays or copies/merges object properties.
whyWrong: The spread operator doesn't create classes.
The spread operator doesn't handle errors, that's the role of try/catch.
The spread operator doesn't delete properties, rest/destructuring with omission handles that differently.

sampleQuestions.question: Which LWC lifecycle hook runs when the component is inserted into the DOM?
sampleQuestions.explanation: connectedCallback runs when the component is added to the DOM.
whyWrong: renderedCallback fires after every render, not specifically on initial DOM insertion.
disconnectedCallback fires when a component is removed from the DOM, not inserted.
errorCallback fires when a descendant component throws an error, unrelated to DOM insertion.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of @wire in LWC?
options: To reactively fetch data or call Apex imperatively with reactive parameters
sampleQuestions.explanation: @wire reactively fetches data when parameters change.
whyWrong: @wire itself doesn't track state, that's the role of @track or reactive properties.
@wire doesn't directly handle DOM events, that's done with event listeners.
@wire is for provisioning data, not for exposing properties to templates (that's @api).

sampleQuestions.question: Which JavaScript method creates a new array from another without mutating the original?
sampleQuestions.explanation: map and slice return new arrays; they don't mutate the original.
whyWrong: push mutates the original array by adding to it.
splice mutates the original array in place.
pop mutates the original array by removing its last element.

sampleQuestions.question: What does event.target refer to in a DOM event handler?
options: The element that dispatched the event
sampleQuestions.explanation: event.target is the element that triggered the event.
whyWrong: event.target is not the window object; window is the global browsing context.
event.target refers to the specific element that fired the event, not the whole document.
event.target is not the parent element; that would require traversing the DOM tree separately.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Aura component attribute type is similar to @api in LWC?
sampleQuestions.explanation: aura:attribute with public/global access exposes data like @api.
whyWrong: aura:method exposes a callable method, not a data property equivalent to @api.
aura:handler registers event handling logic, not a component-facing property.
aura:registerEvent is used to declare that a component can fire an event, not to expose a property.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a JavaScript module?
options: A file that exports bindings for reuse and encapsulates code
sampleQuestions.explanation: Modules export bindings and provide encapsulation via import/export.
whyWrong: A module isn't limited to a single variable; it can export multiple bindings.
A JavaScript module can contain more than a single class, it's a broader unit of code organization.
A module isn't limited to functions alone; it can export any bindings.

sampleQuestions.question: Which LWC method is used to navigate programmatically?
sampleQuestions.explanation: NavigationMixin.GeneratePage enables programmatic navigation in LWC.
whyWrong: history.push is a browser history API concept, not the LWC-specific navigation method.
NavigationMixin is in fact the standard way LWC handles programmatic navigation, this option incorrectly denies its use.
window.location causes a full page reload, which isn't the LWC-recommended navigation approach.

sampleQuestions.question: What does const prevent in JavaScript?
options: Reassignment of the variable binding (but not mutation of objects)
sampleQuestions.explanation: const prevents reassignment; object/array contents can still be mutated.
whyWrong: const has nothing to do with block scope, that behavior comes from let and const equally, not from preventing scope.
const doesn't prevent variable declaration, it's a way of declaring variables.
const does not prevent mutation of the contents of objects/arrays, only reassignment of the binding itself.
